newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: New PNG premier welcomes release of hostages.
newsitem.headline: New PNG premier welcomes release of hostages.

text.p: Newly-elected Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Bill Skate on Thursday welcomed the release of five soldiers held hostage by Bougainville rebels and vowed to step up efforts to end the secessionist revolt.
The five Papua New Guinea soldiers, held captive by Bougainville Revolutionary Army (BRA) rebels since September 1996, were released to New Zealand officials on Thursday.
"I applaud the announcement by the BRA of the...release of the hostages," Skate said in a statement.
"This gesture is in the interests of goodwill and is a show of humanity to the family and friends of the hostages and is a great start to the reconciliation process," Skate said.
The soldiers were released over on board the New Zealand frigate Canterbury, lying off Bougainville, said the New Zealand government in a statement.

New Zealand recently hosted two weeks of peace talks attended by 70 representatives from the Port Moresby-backed Bougainville Interim Government and rebels. The parties agreed to work towards formal peace talks with the Papua New Guinea government starting in September.
Skate, who swept to power on Tuesday, said he planned to appoint a Bougainvillean as minister responsible for the resource-rich island.
"It is my intention to appoint as the minister...a member from Bougainville who is considered by Bougainvilleans to be the best-placed member to liase with all parties involved," he said.

Skate urged rebel leaders to cooperate with renewed peace intiatives and said he would consider putting in place "province-wide political and administrative structures on Bougainville...necessary for peace-building foundations".

Thousands have died in the nine-year conflict on Bougainville, 800 km (500 miles) northeast of Port Moresby, since landowners revolted in 1988 over damage caused by the huge Panguna copper mine and royalties.
"People on Bougainville continue to live under conditions of hardhsip, suffering and unnecessary death," Skate said.

A failed plan to hire African mercenaries to put down the rebellion led to civil and military unrest in March. Voters in last month's elections responded by ousting former prime minister Sir Julius Chan and over 50 sitting parliamentarians.
